L01.materials: Place-value mat, numeral cards, dictation slips
L01.induction: Show 8,050,006. Ask pupils which places are marked with zeros.
L01.model: Model grouping a numeral into millions, thousands and ones. Include 10,000,000 as the upper limit.
L01.guided_practice: Match word cards to numerals, read them to a partner and reconstruct one using place-value cards.
L01.assessment: Read 7,204,060 and 9,080,017. Write six million forty thousand and five using digits.
L01.evidence: Correct readings preserve the thousands groups. The dictated number is 6,040,005.
L01.closure: Ask pupils how the place values distinguish 3,000,040 from 3,040,000.

L02.induction: Display 6,409,050 and 6,509,050. Ask which digit changes and by how much.
L02.model: Build 6,409,050 on a place chart. Write it as a sum, then demonstrate adding or subtracting a repeated place-value amount across a regrouping boundary.
L02.guided_practice: Make one increasing strip with a step of 100,000 and a decreasing one with a step of 10,000. Swap strips, find the gaps and explain how the rule works when a digit changes place.
L02.assessment: Expand 8,760,040. Find the missing term in 8,760,040, 8,740,040, blank, 8,700,040 and the next term. Explain both moves.
L02.evidence: 8,000,000 + 700,000 + 60,000 + 40. The gap is 8,720,040 and the next term is 8,680,040. Subtract 20,000 each time.
L02.closure: Ask pupils to describe the regrouping in the last move.

L03.materials: Fraction strips, reading cards, mock data labels
L03.induction: Show one million as eight equal parts. Ask how many parts a three-eighths label represents.
L03.model: Read fraction-of-a-million labels and show the numerator and denominator on the strip. Use whole and mixed numbers in context.
L03.guided_practice: Label mock records using halves, quarters, fifths, eighths and tenths, then exchange them for oral reading.
L03.assessment: Read 3/4 million and 2 3/5 million. Write one half million, one and five eighths million and four and three tenths million using fractions.
L03.evidence: Read three quarters of a million and two and three fifths million. Written answers are 1/2 million, 1 5/8 million and 4 3/10 million.
L03.closure: Ask how the denominator shows the number of equal parts in one million.

L04.induction: Show 2.075 million and ask what each digit after the decimal point represents.
L04.model: Compare 1.025 million with 1.25 million. Model reading the decimal digits and using zeros as placeholders.
L04.guided_practice: Trade mock attendance reports and predict which value is greatest. Rewrite two whole-number entries in decimal millions.
L04.assessment: Express 4,006,000 and 8,250,000 in decimal millions. Write three point zero eight five million as a numeral in million form.
L04.closure: Ask why 0.06 million and 0.006 million denote different quantities.

L05.materials: Million grids, conversion cards, place chart
L05.induction: Show a tally of 750,000 alongside 3/4 million. Ask how to show they match.
L05.model: Use one million as the whole for both fraction and decimal conversions. Divide by one million to reverse the direction.
L05.guided_practice: Sort triple-matching cards with whole-number, fraction-million and decimal-million forms. Build new triples and show one reversible conversion across equivalent forms.
L05.assessment: Convert 3 3/8 million and 2.048 million to whole numbers. Convert 2,750,000 to fraction millions and check it in decimal millions.
L05.evidence: 3,375,000 and 2,048,000. The reverse pair is 2 3/4 million and 2.75 million.
L05.closure: Ask pupils to name the common whole used in each conversion.

L06.materials: Number-line strips, stock cards, place chart
L06.induction: Show 1.4 million and 350,000. Ask how to put both in the same form.
L06.model: Convert quantities to the same unit before adding or subtracting. Demonstrate checking a difference by addition.
L06.guided_practice: Solve one stock total and one stock balance using whole numbers, then express the results in millions.
L06.assessment: Find 1.45 million + 325,000 and 2 1/2 million − 0.375 million. Give both answers as whole numbers and check the difference.
L06.closure: Ask when converting to whole numbers makes the alignment clearer.

L07.materials: Group mats, meeting cards, multiplication and division grids
L07.induction: Ask how many groups of 0.25 million make one million.
L07.model: Represent multiplication as equal groups and division as finding group size or number of groups. Check one result through the inverse operation.
L07.guided_practice: Build both multiplication and division cards for matched groups. Compare calculations in whole numbers, fractions of a million and decimal millions.
L07.assessment: Find three times 0.625 million. Divide 2 1/2 million equally among five centres. Use multiplication to verify one centre's share.
L07.closure: Ask which units belong to a total and to a share.

L08.induction: Show 3 × (0.45 + 0.2) million and ask which operation comes first.
L08.model: Compare the bracketed expression with 3 × 0.45 million + 0.2 million. Label the first operation in each.
L08.guided_practice: Mark the first operation in two expressions and explain their decision to a partner.
L08.assessment: Evaluate 2.7 million − 3 × 0.4 million and (2.7 million − 0.4 million) × 3. State the first step in each.
L08.evidence: 1.5 million and 6.9 million. Multiply first in the first expression and subtract first in the second.
L08.closure: Ask how brackets move the subtraction before multiplication.

L09.induction: Show four equal groups and one unknown amount in each. Ask what the letter represents.
L09.model: Write 2 × (n + 0.35 million) = 2 million. Reverse the outer operation first and use substitution to check.
L09.guided_practice: Work through one multiplication-and-addition equation with the unknown inside brackets and another with the unknown outside.
L09.assessment: Solve 4 × (n + 0.125 million) = 1.8 million and 3 × p + 0.1 million = 1.3 million. Substitute to check both.
L09.evidence: n = 0.325 million and p = 0.4 million. Checks give 1.8 million and 1.3 million.
L09.closure: Ask why subtraction comes before division in solving the second equation.

L10.induction: Build one 3 × 3 array and one single row for nine counters. Ask what each shows.
L10.model: Compare factor pairs of 29, 49 and 45. Explain the definition of a prime and use it to explain the status of 1.
L10.guided_practice: Use factor ladders and arrays to classify numbers. Compare a prime near 100, a non-square composite and a square with an identical factor pair.
L10.assessment: Classify 43, 49, 51 and 1. List their factor pairs and identify which number has exactly two distinct factors.
L10.evidence: 43 is prime (1 × 43). 49 and 51 are composite (1 × 49 and 7 × 7, 1 × 51 and 3 × 17). The number 1 has only one factor and is neither prime nor composite.
L10.closure: Ask why a product of two copies of 7 establishes that 49 is composite.

L11.materials: Stock cards, group diagram, mixed-operation strips
L11.induction: Ask how a shipment count written as a fraction of a million can be compared with whole-number stock.
L11.model: Model finding a stock balance with different forms of a million. Then use factor pairs to decide how to split a small stock equally.
L11.guided_practice: Choose a calculation for a stock scenario and test the proposed group sizes in a second situation.
L11.assessment: A warehouse has 2 1/2 million pens, sends out 0.7 million and 3/8 million, and shares the remainder among five centres. Find each share. Choose 37 or 42 packs to split into equal groups with at least two groups of two or more.
L11.evidence: 285,000 pens per centre. Choose 42, for example 6 × 7. The only factor pair for 37 is 1 × 37.
L11.closure: Ask pupils how they can verify one centre's share.

R01.materials: Brackets cards, worked-error slips, place-value chart
R01.induction: Show the incorrect statement 8 − 2 × 3 = 18. Ask pupils to mark the first operation.
R01.model: Review marking the first operation in an expression and show how to check the result by reworking in whole numbers.
R01.guided_practice: Correct a worked example and explain the point where the calculations diverge.
R01.assessment: Correct 2.4 million − 0.6 million ÷ 3 if someone divides last. Then find (1.8 million − 0.3 million) ÷ 5 and check by multiplication.
R01.evidence: 2.2 million and 0.3 million. The last check is 0.3 million × 5 = 1.5 million.
R01.closure: Ask under what condition subtraction would come first in the first example.

L12.materials: Fraction bars, fraction cards, squared paper
L12.induction: Ask how many quarters are in three quarters.
L12.model: Show 3/4 ÷ 3 on a bar and explain sharing. Compare with 3/4 ÷ 1/4 as finding how many groups fit.
L12.guided_practice: Draw one sharing example and solve a mixed-number example by converting to an improper fraction first.
L12.assessment: Draw 3/4 ÷ 3. Find 2 2/3 ÷ 4/9 and verify the quotient by multiplication.
L12.closure: Ask how the meaning of the divisor changes between the two examples.

L13.induction: Ask whether 0.6 × 0.4 is more or less than half.
L13.model: Use the overlap of two decimal strips to explain hundredths. For a longer product, estimate and then calculate the exact decimal.
L13.guided_practice: Use grids for tenths and a written algorithm for longer decimals. Compare estimates and exact values and explain when removing a final zero preserves the value.
L13.assessment: Estimate and find 0.75 × 0.4, 1.25 × 0.6 and 0.35 × 0.14. Explain where the point is placed in one answer.
L13.evidence: 0.3, 0.75 and 0.049. 0.35 × 0.14 gives 0.0490 before dropping the final zero.
L13.closure: Ask why the first product is smaller than 0.75.

L14.materials: Place-value charts, quotient cards, long-division grids
L14.induction: Show 4.2 ÷ 0.7 and ask how to make 0.7 a whole number without changing the quotient.
L14.model: Multiply both the dividend and divisor by the same power of ten. Demonstrate one calculation and verify the result by multiplying back.
L14.guided_practice: Sort equivalent divisions, then estimate and solve those with one- and two-place divisors. Compare work and check a quotient with three decimal places.
L14.assessment: Find 5.04 ÷ 0.12, 0.84 ÷ 0.4 and 3.45 ÷ 1.2. Record the equivalent divisions and verify the last result.
L14.evidence: 42, 2.1 and 2.875. Equivalent divisions are 504 ÷ 12, 8.4 ÷ 4 and 34.5 ÷ 12. Check 2.875 × 1.2 = 3.45.
L14.closure: Ask pupils to explain why the power of ten must be the same for both numbers.

L15.materials: Hundred grids, matching cards, place-value mats
L15.induction: Shade one full grid and 28% of a second. Ask how much is shown.
L15.model: Connect one whole to 100% and model changing 1.28 to 128%. Reverse by dividing the percentage number by 100.
L15.guided_practice: Match decimal and percentage cards. Justify one equivalence with a grid or a number line.
L15.assessment: Convert 2.075 and 1.28 to percentages, then 165% and 235.5% to decimals. Explain one match.
L15.evidence: 207.5%, 128%, 1.65 and 2.355. The conversion uses the meaning of per hundred.
L15.closure: Ask pupils to show why any percentage above 100 gives a decimal above one.

L16.induction: Show two sectors labelled 35% and 27% on one chart. Ask which total they refer to.
L16.model: Add and subtract percentages referring to a common base. Distinguish a difference in percentage points from a percentage change.
L16.guided_practice: Write expressions for combining two categories and finding how much of the whole is unused.
L16.assessment: Find 85% + 42%, 178% − 36.5% and the difference between 35% and 27% as percentage points.
L16.closure: Ask which starting quantity the percentages refer to.

L17.materials: Double number lines, scale tables, quantity cards
L17.induction: Place 6.4 kg on the 100% line. Ask what quantity represents 25%.
L17.model: Find 125% by combining 100% with 25%. Reverse the method by dividing the comparison quantity by the reference quantity.
L17.guided_practice: Complete quantity and percent tables in both directions. Test examples below and above 100% and label the reference quantity in each.
L17.assessment: Find 125% of 6.4 kg and 75% of 4.8 L. Find the percentages represented by 7.5 L of 6 L and 1.26 kg of 1.8 kg.
L17.evidence: 8 kg, 3.6 L, 125% and 70%. The reference quantity is correctly identified in each case.
L17.closure: Ask why comparing 7.5 L with 6 L gives a result greater than 100%.

L18.materials: Bracket cards, fraction bars, operation strips
L18.induction: Compare 5.5 − (1 1/2 + 0.75) with the same expression without brackets.
L18.model: Convert between decimals and fractions where it simplifies a calculation. Show how brackets affect the first step and how to check the result by estimating.
L18.guided_practice: Solve paired examples with two distinct operations. Underline the first operation, compare routes and explain why a result is reasonable.
L18.assessment: Find 5.5 − (1 1/2 + 0.75), 3/4 + 2.4 × 0.5 and 2 ÷ (0.25 × 8). Show the first step for each.
L18.evidence: 3.25, 1.95 and 1. The first steps give 2.25, 1.2 and 2 respectively.
L18.closure: Ask when writing 3/4 as a decimal makes a mixed calculation easier.

L19.induction: Ask whether the result of 4 × (2.5 − 3/4) should be above or below 10.
L19.model: Compare an estimate with the exact result. Then model checking a mixed division and multiplication by estimating both factors.
L19.guided_practice: Solve the same expression in fractions and decimals, then select the more efficient route and justify it.
L19.assessment: Find 4 × (2.5 − 3/4) and 3/4 + 2.4 ÷ 0.6. Show the first operation and a sensible estimate for one expression.
L19.evidence: 7 and 4.75. Rounding 2.5 − 3/4 to about 2 gives an estimate near 8 for the first expression.
L19.closure: Ask why the exact result differs from that estimate.

L20.materials: Tank bars, fraction and percentage labels, measuring chart
L20.induction: Show a portion labelled 25% and ask which fraction gives the same amount.
L20.model: Represent a percent and a fraction on the same whole. Then show how to compare an equal share to a known capacity.
L20.guided_practice: Break two situations into known quantities and an unknown. Mark whether the percentage or fraction refers to the original quantity.
L20.assessment: From 48 kg, 25% is sold and 1/3 of the original mass is donated. Find the remainder. Divide 10.8 L among nine 1.5 L jugs. Give each amount as a percent of capacity.
L20.evidence: 20 kg remains. Each jug holds 1.2 L, or 80% of capacity.
L20.closure: Ask why one problem uses 48 kg as the base and the other uses 1.5 L.

R02.materials: Fraction error cards, percent charts, decimal grids
R02.induction: Show 120% labelled 0.12. Ask how a grid can help check it.
R02.model: Revisit dividing fractions and finding the reference quantity in a percentage comparison. Model identifying an error from its estimate.
R02.guided_practice: Rotate through fraction, decimal and percentage stations. Correct a partner's calculation and annotate the step that caused the error.
R02.assessment: Correct 5/6 ÷ 5/9 if shown as 25/54. Then compare 4.5 L with 3.6 L as a percent, and check 3.45 ÷ 1.2 by multiplication.
R02.evidence: 1 1/2, 125% and 2.875. The first operation uses 9/5 as the reciprocal. 2.875 × 1.2 = 3.45.
R02.closure: Ask which two estimates help identify the fraction and percentage errors before solving.

L21.induction: Show cost RM28 and selling price RM35. Ask what each amount describes.
L21.model: Label cost price and selling price. Use the direction of the difference to distinguish profit and loss.
L21.guided_practice: Sort sample transactions into profit and loss. Explain which figures show the amount paid for stock and the amount received from sales.
L21.assessment: A seller pays RM28 and receives RM35 for item A, and pays RM42 and receives RM39 for item B. Label both prices and identify each profit or loss.
L21.evidence: A has cost RM28, selling price RM35 and profit RM7. B has cost RM42, selling price RM39 and loss RM3.
L21.closure: Ask what happens when the cost and selling price are equal.

L22.materials: Fictional offer cards, bill, receipt and invoice samples
L22.induction: Show an instant price reduction and cash returned after purchase. Ask when each reduction takes effect.
L22.model: Compare discounts, rebates and vouchers. Show a bill requesting payment, an invoice listing a transaction and a receipt acknowledging payment. Point out the example tax line.
L22.guided_practice: At stations, annotate the original price, offer type, document purpose and tax line. Justify why an invoice and a receipt convey different information.
L22.assessment: Name an instant 15% reduction, RM20 returned after purchase and a RM10 coupon. Match a monthly request, an itemised amount due and proof of payment with the three documents. Find the line marked service tax on the sample.
L22.evidence: Discount, rebate, voucher. Bill, invoice, receipt. The service tax is the labelled amount on the sample.
L22.closure: Ask why a receipt can help verify that a billed amount has been paid.

L23.materials: Financial scenario cards, two-column sort sheet
L23.induction: Give examples of cash saved and an amount still owed on a loan. Ask how they differ.
L23.model: Distinguish assets and liabilities. Compare interest credited to a savings account with a distribution to holders of an investment.
L23.guided_practice: Sort examples of property, savings and unpaid obligations. Label returns on two fictional statements.
L23.assessment: Classify RM400 in savings and an RM80 unpaid borrowing balance. Identify a return paid on a savings balance and a distribution to shareholders.
L23.evidence: Savings are an asset and the unpaid balance is a liability. The returns are interest and a dividend respectively.
L23.closure: Ask which example represents money that still has to be paid.

L24.materials: Price comparison table, fictional sale cards
L24.induction: Show a selling price and a profit. Ask how to recover the cost.
L24.model: Use the difference between selling and cost prices. Compare when a discount is deducted and when a rebate is returned.
L24.guided_practice: Find a missing price in a sale card. Record both the amount paid today and the effective cost for each offer.
L24.assessment: A seller receives RM92 and makes RM17 profit. Find the cost. For a RM200 item, compare 15% off immediately with RM36 rebated after paying full price.
L24.evidence: Cost RM75. Immediate discount gives RM170. The rebate gives an effective cost of RM164, with RM200 paid first.
L24.closure: Ask why the amount paid at the counter may differ from the effective cost.

L25.materials: Fictional receipt, savings and dividend cards, percent strips
L25.induction: Show three sample rates. Ask which starting amount belongs to each calculation.
L25.model: Define a separate base for a tax on a service, interest for one year and a dividend on a fictional investment. Show how each value can be checked with a percent strip.
L25.guided_practice: Work through three fictional statements. Underline each base, write the amount produced by the rate, then contrast it with the ending or total amount.
L25.assessment: Use a sample rate of 6% on a RM95 service, 2% for one year on RM800 savings and 4% on a RM1,500 investment. Give tax, total service charge, interest and dividend.
L25.evidence: Tax RM5.70. Service total RM100.70. Interest RM16. Dividend RM60. Each percentage is applied to its stated base.
L25.closure: Ask why the tax is added to the service charge in the example.

L26.materials: Fictional protection cards, risk and scenario matrix
L26.induction: Show a travel disruption and damage to a home. Ask what unexpected costs each could generate.
L26.model: Introduce insurance and takaful as protection arrangements with specified risks, limits and terms. Describe a takaful contribution to a shared fund.
L26.guided_practice: Match fictional arrangements to risks, compare the benefits and limits on sample cards, and identify one situation outside each example's stated scope.
L26.assessment: Match a travel card covering specified medical costs and a home card covering fire damage with their two scenarios. Explain one purpose of protection and what a stated limit means.
L26.evidence: Match travel medical expenses to the travel card and fire damage to the home card. Protection helps with specified financial costs. A limit is the maximum under the example terms.
L26.closure: Ask why checking the risk described on the card matters before relying on a benefit.

L27.materials: Two fictional supplier quotes, budget worksheet
L27.induction: Show a supplier's item cost and a service charge. Ask what belongs in the complete comparison.
L27.model: Separate costs, one-time charges, stated example tax and any later rebate. Compare immediate cash outlay and effective cost with the budget.
L27.guided_practice: Evaluate two supplier cards, check totals independently and consider one practical risk such as a late rebate.
L27.assessment: A club has RM320 available now. Option A costs RM260 plus RM50 service taxed at 6%. Option B costs RM330 now and returns RM24 later. Find both initial and effective totals and justify an option.
L27.evidence: A costs RM313 now and in total. B costs RM330 initially and RM306 after rebate. A fits available funds today. B depends on extra upfront funds and later rebate.
L27.closure: Ask how a delayed rebate affects a budget decision even if the final cost is lower.

R03.materials: Fictional receipt, budget and offer cards
R03.induction: Show a receipt with separate item, service and service-tax lines. Ask which base should be used.
R03.model: Review reading the receipt and verifying a stated rate. Compare the resulting total with available money.
R03.guided_practice: Check a partner's receipt and record which amount supports a budget conclusion.
R03.assessment: A sample receipt shows RM185 for goods and RM50 service with 6% tax on service. Check the total and the balance from RM250.
R03.evidence: Tax RM3, total RM238 and balance RM12. The base is RM50.
R03.closure: Ask when the goods price would belong in a different tax calculation.

L28.materials: Time-zone map, UTC reference line, model clocks
L28.induction: Show two local clocks for the same event. Ask how their readings can differ.
L28.model: Use the Greenwich reference and explain positive and negative UTC offsets. Associate each offset with the local clock at the same instant.
L28.guided_practice: Locate two stated offsets on a simplified time-zone map. Set model clocks to show simultaneous local times.
L28.assessment: Locate labelled regions UTC+8 and UTC−3. If UTC is 12:00, give local times for both regions and explain the offset signs.
L28.evidence: 20:00 and 09:00 on the same day. The plus sign indicates ahead of UTC and the minus sign indicates behind UTC.
L28.closure: Ask what UTC+0 shows for the same event.

L29.materials: UTC cards, 24-hour number lines, clock models
L29.induction: Show UTC+8 and UTC−4. Ask how their signs affect the difference.
L29.model: Place both on a UTC number line. Model finding the difference and converting across midnight, including a half-hour offset.
L29.guided_practice: Solve three pairs using positive, negative and fractional offsets. Check each by converting both clocks to UTC.
L29.assessment: If Q at UTC−4 shows Tuesday 16:45, give the time and day at P at UTC+8. If A at UTC+9 shows 16:00, give the time at B at UTC+5:30.
L29.evidence: P is Wednesday 04:45, 12 hours ahead of Q. B is 12:30 on the same day, 3 hours 30 minutes behind A.
L29.closure: Ask how converting both local times to UTC checks the first answer.

L30.materials: Two-city clocks, flight cards, weekly timeline
L30.induction: Show a flight departure and duration. Ask when the destination time-zone adjustment is applied.
L30.model: Add actual travel time first, then convert the resulting time to the destination zone. Show how to choose an overlapping daytime call time.
L30.guided_practice: Plan one journey and one call using fixed offsets. Recheck both day changes and whether the call meets each person's availability.
L30.assessment: A flight leaves UTC+8 Wednesday at 20:15, lasts 6 hours 40 minutes, and lands at UTC+3. Give local arrival. A call begins Monday 15:30 at UTC+8 for 75 minutes. Give start and end at UTC+1 and check a local 08:00–10:00 availability window.
L30.evidence: At departure it is Wednesday 15:15 at UTC+3. Add 6 h 40 min to reach Wednesday 21:55. The call is Monday 08:30 to 09:45 at UTC+1, within the availability window.
L30.closure: Ask pupils to distinguish the elapsed flight duration from the destination clock difference.

R04.materials: Model clocks, fixed-time-zone schedule, error slip
R04.induction: Show a journey arriving just after midnight in its origin zone. Ask whether the destination must show the same date.
R04.model: Review marking day changes before and after converting time zones. Check a proposed entry on a two-city schedule.
R04.guided_practice: Correct the day or time on a partner's sample itinerary and identify the error.
R04.assessment: A call starts Tuesday 23:20 at UTC−2 and lasts 50 minutes. A schedule records it as Tuesday 06:20 to 07:10 at UTC+5. Correct the date and verify the time.
R04.evidence: The UTC+5 clock shows Wednesday 06:20 to 07:10. The zones differ by seven hours.
R04.closure: Ask what would change if the second zone were seven hours behind instead.

L31.materials: Ribbon or wire samples, scale, metre ruler, measurement cards
L31.induction: Show two lengths of the same material. Ask how to compare their masses fairly.
L31.model: Use the stated uniform mass per metre to scale a length. Convert centimetres to metres before applying the rate.
L31.guided_practice: Complete a rate table for two lengths. Solve the reverse problem and check that the result is a length.
L31.assessment: Ribbon has a uniform mass of 24 g per 2 m. Find the mass of 750 cm. A wire sample weighs 300 g per 4 m. Find the length of 450 g in cm.
L31.evidence: Ribbon 90 g using 12 g per metre. Wire length 600 cm using 75 g per metre.
L31.closure: Ask which rate belongs to each material.

L32.materials: Same-bore hose diagrams, measuring jug, litre table
L32.induction: Show equal sections cut from the same size hose. Ask why equal lengths can contain the same volume.
L32.model: Use volume per metre for a uniform hose. Check proportional scaling with a table and convert mL to L.
L32.guided_practice: Compare converting before and after multiplying. Solve one reverse question for length given a volume.
L32.assessment: A uniform hose holds 600 mL in 4 m. Find how many litres 7 m holds and how many metres hold 0.9 L.
L32.evidence: 1.05 L for 7 m and 6 m for 0.9 L, using 150 mL per metre.
L32.closure: Ask why both hoses must have the same internal size for this comparison.

L33.materials: Recipe cards, scale, measuring jug, proportional tables
L33.induction: Show a recipe quantity for one mix. Ask how the mass changes when the measured liquid triples.
L33.model: Use a given relationship for a specific mix. Compare scaling both quantities together with a unit-rate calculation.
L33.guided_practice: Build a mass-and-volume table for three batches. Check by converting grams to kilograms and solving one reverse quantity problem.
L33.assessment: A mix uses 240 g flour for 0.6 L of water. Find the mass for 1.5 L in g and kg. Then find the water volume required for 720 g at the same ratio.
L33.evidence: 600 g or 0.6 kg. 720 g requires 1.8 L. Both quantities are scaled using the stated recipe.
L33.closure: Ask which assumption allows the same ratio to be applied to each batch.

R05.materials: Error cards, metric conversion chart, rate table
R05.induction: Show a report that treats 750 cm as 0.75 m. Ask pupils to check the conversion.
R05.model: Review matching units before scaling. Model checking whether the final answer should be a length, mass or volume.
R05.guided_practice: Correct two worked errors, identifying the incorrect factor and writing the proper unit.
R05.assessment: Correct an estimate of 9 g for 750 cm of wire when 2 m weighs 24 g. Then find the water volume for 540 g if 180 g uses 0.45 L.
R05.evidence: 750 cm is 7.5 m, so the wire weighs 90 g. Three batches use 1.35 L.
R05.closure: Ask why labelling the rate with both units can reveal a scaling mistake.

L34.induction: Show a baseline and ask where the protractor centre and zero should align.
L34.model: Model a 65° angle, then rotate the starting ray and show how to choose the correct protractor scale.
L34.guided_practice: Draw an acute and an obtuse angle from rays in different directions. Trade and measure a partner's construction.
L34.assessment: Draw 45° and 130° with labelled vertices and rays. Measure both after construction.
L34.evidence: The angles are within 2° of the target. Each measurement starts from the zero aligned with its first ray.
L34.closure: Ask why choosing the other scale can turn an acute angle into an obtuse one.

L35.materials: Triangular and square grids, protractors, geometry software
L35.induction: Show an equilateral triangle and a stretched hexagon. Ask how measurements can establish regularity.
L35.model: Build an equilateral triangle on a triangular grid and a square on a square grid. Use a regular-polygon tool for an octagon.
L35.guided_practice: Draw a triangle and a square on appropriate grids. Construct an octagon digitally, measure two sides and compare adjacent interior angles.
L35.assessment: Submit the three constructions. Label the number of sides, mark the equal sides and measure two interior angles of each.
L35.evidence: Equilateral triangle 60°, square 90° and regular octagon 135° within 2°. Check side lengths and correct number of sides.
L35.closure: Ask which checks still matter when a figure looks regular on screen.

L36.materials: Circle templates, paper discs, rulers, labels
L36.induction: Fold a paper disc along two different diameters. Ask what the intersection represents.
L36.model: Label the centre, a segment from centre to circumference and a segment through the centre joining two points on the circumference. Compare radius and diameter.
L36.guided_practice: Measure radii and diameters of three circular templates. Draw a chord that misses the centre and explain why it is different.
L36.assessment: On the teacher's diagram, P is the centre, AB goes through P, and CD misses P. Label centre, a radius and diameter. Calculate the diameter if PA is 4.5 cm.
L36.evidence: Centre P, radius PA or PB, diameter AB. Diameter 9 cm. CD is a chord that does not go through P.
L36.closure: Ask what makes every diameter twice the radius.

L37.induction: Ask how far apart the compass legs should be for a radius of 3.2 cm.
L37.model: Set the distance with a ruler, keep the point fixed, and draw the circle. Label the centre and choose diameter endpoints on a line through it.
L37.guided_practice: Draw one circle and exchange it with a partner to check the radius and diameter. Construct a second circle from a different radius.
L37.assessment: Draw a circle of radius 3.2 cm. Label the centre O, radius OA and diameter AB. Measure and report the diameter.
L37.evidence: Radius 3.2 cm and diameter 6.4 cm within 1 mm. A, O and B lie on the same line.
L37.closure: Ask which measurement can catch an incorrect compass setting.

L38.induction: Show a circular lid near a square opening. Ask which dimension determines whether it fits.
L38.model: Compare a circle's diameter with the width of the opening. Draw a simple scale sketch to explain the clearance.
L38.guided_practice: Sketch two width choices. Mark the widest part of the lid and compare it with both openings.
L38.assessment: A lid of radius 14 cm must fit in a 27 cm or 29 cm square opening. Pick the one that works and find the total spare width. Show it in a sketch.
L38.evidence: Diameter 28 cm. The 29 cm opening works and has 1 cm total spare width.
L38.closure: Ask how much clearance lies on each side if the lid is centred.

R06.materials: Compasses, rulers, protractors, circle and ray cards
R06.induction: Show two circles with different radii. Ask what measurements allow a fair comparison.
R06.model: Review selecting a compass width and checking a diameter. Revisit placing the protractor zero on a starting ray.
R06.guided_practice: Swap labelled diagrams and verify a diameter or angle. Explain one correction using the correct instrument.
R06.assessment: Draw two circles with radii 2 cm and 3.5 cm. Compare their diameters. Draw a 110° angle and check it with a protractor.
R06.evidence: Diameters 4 cm and 7 cm, with difference 3 cm. The angle is within 2° of 110°.
R06.closure: Ask which measurement is checked with a ruler and which uses a protractor.

L39.induction: Show a path with horizontal and vertical segments. Ask what the axes and grid scale tell us.
L39.model: Count coordinate intervals separately and multiply by distance per interval. Include a map whose scale gives the distance for two grid intervals.
L39.guided_practice: Plot routes for two scales. Find distances in different units and compare the effect of a changed scale on the same pair of points.
L39.assessment: Plot A(2, 3) and B(7, 6) at 20 m per unit. Then use 250 m per unit for C(2, 1) to D(2, 6). Give both components for each pair.
L39.evidence: A–B horizontally 100 m and vertically 60 m. C–D horizontally 0 m and vertically 1,250 m.
L39.closure: Ask pupils why a vertical movement leaves x unchanged.

L40.materials: Two-colour counters, ratio strips, factor charts
L40.induction: Show 24 red and 36 white counters. Ask what group size could divide both counts exactly.
L40.model: Write the ordered ratio. Divide both terms by a common factor and check whether the resulting terms share another factor.
L40.guided_practice: Build equivalent ratios with counters, reduce them and swap the language of the quantities to see how the order changes.
L40.assessment: Simplify 24 red to 36 white, then 45 blue to 30 green. Check if 18 : 27 is equivalent to the first ratio.
L40.evidence: 2 : 3 and 3 : 2. 18 : 27 also reduces to 2 : 3. Both terms have been divided by the same factor.
L40.closure: Ask which change would reverse the order without changing the quantities.

L41.materials: Ratio tables, recipe cards, bar diagrams
L41.induction: Show three cups of concentrate for five of water. Ask how much water pairs with double the concentrate.
L41.model: Build a ratio table and apply the same factor to both columns. Model finding one part when a total and ratio are given.
L41.guided_practice: Complete two tables and compare unit-value and scale-factor methods. Use a bar model for a total split.
L41.assessment: For 3 cups concentrate to 5 cups water, find the water for 12 cups concentrate and the concentrate for 30 cups water. Split 64 pupils in the ratio 3 : 5.
L41.evidence: 20 cups water and 18 cups concentrate. The groups are 24 and 40 pupils, with eight per part.
L41.closure: Ask how checking the original ratio detects a one-column scaling error.

L42.induction: Show a two-segment route and a recipe table. Ask what the scale means in each.
L42.model: Work a horizontal and vertical distance using a given scale. Compare unit value with ratio parts in a daily mixing problem.
L42.guided_practice: Group the information on each problem card, choose a grid or ratio table and verify units.
L42.assessment: Travel from (1, 2) to (5, 7) horizontally then vertically at 30 m per unit. Give both distances. Mix 18 L in the ratio 2 parts concentrate to 7 parts water. Find both volumes.
L42.evidence: 120 m horizontal and 150 m vertical. Mixture needs 4 L concentrate and 14 L water.
L42.closure: Ask pupils which totals check the two solutions.

R07.materials: Coordinate grid, timeline ruler, ratio error cards
R07.induction: Show a grid whose scale is two intervals for 60 m. Ask the distance per interval.
R07.model: Review counting intervals instead of grid lines. Check proportional tables by comparing scale factors in both columns.
R07.guided_practice: Correct one grid distance and one table with a missing quantity. Describe the error and show a working check.
R07.assessment: A(2, 4) to B(8, 4) is listed as 60 m at 30 m per grid unit. Correct it. At a fixed rate, 6 books cost RM48. Find the cost of 15 books and show a ratio table.
R07.evidence: A–B is 180 m horizontal and 0 m vertical. Books cost RM120 using RM8 per book.
R07.closure: Ask how either answer can be verified by working backward.

L43.materials: Blank circles marked at the centre, rulers, protractors, survey cards
L43.induction: Show a semicircle and a quarter circle. Ask what fraction of a survey each would represent.
L43.model: Use the given counts to find halves, quarters and eighths. Convert those fractions to 180°, 90° and 45° sectors.
L43.guided_practice: Complete two survey charts, label sectors and check that each angle total is 360°. Compare sectors using both angle and number of pupils.
L43.assessment: Of 40 pupils, 20 choose A, 10 B, five C and five D. Complete and label a pie chart and compare A with C.
L43.evidence: Sector angles 180°, 90°, 45° and 45°. A exceeds C by 15 pupils. The angles total 360°.
L43.closure: Ask what the equal sectors for C and D tell us about the counts.

L44.materials: Opaque bags, coloured counters, prediction chart
L44.induction: Show seven blue counters and one green counter going into an opaque bag. Ask which colour is likely on one draw.
L44.model: Link relative numbers of equal-sized counters to likely and unlikely outcomes. Use one-draw conditions and compare predictions with trial results.
L44.guided_practice: Make predictions for two pictured bags. Draw with replacement, tally results and explain why a short trial may vary from a prediction.
L44.assessment: Bag A has seven blue and one green counter. Bag B has two blue and six green. For one random draw from each, state whether blue is likely or unlikely and explain.
L44.evidence: Blue is likely in A, where seven of eight are blue. Blue is unlikely in B, where only two of eight are blue.
L44.closure: Ask why an unlikely colour can still appear on a draw.

L45.materials: Equal-sector spinner, labelled counter bags, likelihood scale
L45.induction: Show a spinner with equal sectors for two colours. Ask where that event belongs on a likelihood scale.
L45.model: Place impossible, less likely, equally likely, more likely and certain on a line. Use counts of equally possible outcomes to justify placement.
L45.guided_practice: Classify events from bags and dice. Compare a pair of events with the same likelihood from different models.
L45.assessment: A bag has three red and five blue counters. Classify drawing green, red, blue and either red or blue. For a fair six-face die, classify an even result compared with odd.
L45.evidence: Green impossible, red less likely, blue more likely and red or blue certain. Even and odd are equally likely, with three faces each.
L45.closure: Ask which wording signals a comparison with the other possible outcome.

L46.materials: Bar chart of survey counts, comparison cards, probability strips
L46.induction: Show one category with the tallest bar. Ask what conclusion the chart supports.
L46.model: Read category counts and totals. Show how to compare a category across different sample sizes using its share of the total.
L46.guided_practice: Use two bar charts to make and explain predictions. Check whether a larger count always means a larger share.
L46.assessment: A survey shows 12 story, six comic and two atlas choices. Pick a response at random and describe atlas likelihood. Compare green selections of four out of eight in A and five out of 12 in B.
L46.evidence: Atlas is less likely than either other category, with two of 20 choices. Green is more likely in A because 4/8 exceeds 5/12.
L46.closure: Ask why the larger green count in B does not give the larger share.

R08.materials: Pie-chart cards, matching survey labels, likelihood scale
R08.induction: Show a half-sector and an eighth-sector. Ask which responses would be more common in that survey.
R08.model: Review fractions of a full chart and compare likelihood when selecting one response. Verify that all sectors add to one whole.
R08.guided_practice: Interpret two teacher-made charts. Convert sector sizes to counts and correct one unsupported likelihood claim.
R08.assessment: A chart of 40 responses shows 180° for A, 90° for B and 45° each for C and D. Give all four counts. Explain whether A is more likely than all the others combined.
R08.evidence: 20, 10, five and five. A and the three other categories together have 20 each, so they are equally likely.
R08.closure: Ask which category pairs have equal likelihood when one response is selected.
